scenario.context: The player enters the Hearthstone Tavern in the village of Dunmore, where a group of farmers is discussing the recent harvest failure of their neighbour, Old Gareth. Gareth's fields yielded almost nothing this season, while everyone else had a decent crop. The player overhears Nessa, a prominent local farmer, holding court at the bar.
scenario.text: Nessa shakes her head and takes a long drink. 'Gareth's fields came up empty again. No surprise there — the man is lazy. Always has been. You don't see him out before dawn like the rest of us. He'd rather sit on his porch whittling than work his rows.' A younger farmer, Pell, speaks up quietly: 'Didn't a blight hit the south plots this year? Gareth's land is all south-facing.' Nessa waves him off. 'Blight or no blight, a real farmer finds a way. When my north field flooded last spring, I re-dug the drainage in two days. That's the difference between someone who cares and someone who doesn't.'
scenario.speaker_context: Nessa is a hard-working, respected farmer who genuinely believes effort determines outcomes. She does not notice that she explains her own setback (flooding) by citing an external event she overcame, while explaining Gareth's setback by citing his character.

structure.pattern_description: Nessa attributes Gareth's poor harvest to his character (laziness, lack of care) while ignoring a situational factor (south-facing blight). When her own field flooded, she cited the external event (flooding) and her response to it. She judges others by disposition and herself by situation.
structure.formal_form: Other person's negative outcome -> attributed to character trait. Own negative outcome -> attributed to situational factor. The asymmetry is applied automatically and without reflection.
structure.why_wrong: Gareth's harvest failure has a plausible situational explanation (blight on south-facing land) that Nessa dismisses without investigation. She applies a double standard: her flood was just bad luck she overcame, but Gareth's blight is evidence of who he is. The disposition inference leaps past the available evidence.
structure.counterpoint: Sometimes character really is the explanation. If Gareth had been warned about the blight and refused to take preventive measures that were readily available, Nessa's judgment might be partly warranted. The error is not in ever attributing outcomes to character, but in doing so reflexively while exempting oneself from the same standard.

assessment.identification_prompt: Nessa seems pretty confident about why Gareth's harvest failed. But listen to how she talks about her own flooding problem. Do you notice anything different about how she explains the two situations?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Nessa that Gareth is simply lazy and sees no problem.
Player feels Nessa is being harsh but cannot articulate the asymmetry.
Player notices Nessa is ignoring the blight but does not connect it to the double standard with her own flooding.
Player identifies the asymmetry: Nessa explains Gareth's failure by character but her own setback by situation, and recognizes this as unfair.

Player identifies the fundamental attribution error by name or description, explains the actor-observer asymmetry, and can articulate when character-based explanations might be warranted versus when they are premature.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: When Nessa's north field flooded, she blamed the weather and praised her own response. When Gareth's south field failed, she blamed him. What if you swapped the two — would Nessa say Gareth was just unlucky?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good catch. Now think about this: why do you think people tend to explain their own failures differently from how they explain other people's failures? What makes this asymmetry so natural that Nessa doesn't even notice she's doing it?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Nessa is blunt, hard-working, and proud of her self-reliance. She is not malicious but is deeply invested in the belief that effort determines outcomes. She speaks with the confidence of someone who has never questioned her own explanatory framework.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You want to know why some folks prosper and some don't? It's simple. Some people get up before the sun and some people don't. That's the whole story.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the asymmetry, Nessa pauses and grudgingly admits she never actually checked whether the blight reached Gareth's fields. She agrees to walk the south plots with the player. When they find clear evidence of blight damage, Nessa goes quiet and later brings Gareth a basket of seed grain without explanation.

scenario.context: The player arrives at the Cartographers' Guild in the city of Veranthos. The Guild is preparing an expedition to map the uncharted Thornveil Marshes. Master Cartographer Lirel has spent thirty years mapping difficult terrain and is reviewing applications from volunteers. The player witnesses an exchange between Lirel and a young applicant named Dax, who completed a six-week surveying course last month.
scenario.text: Dax spreads a hand-drawn map on the table with a flourish. 'I mapped the entire Greenvale basin in two weeks. My instructor said it was the fastest anyone had finished the exercise. I'm ready for the Thornveil.' Lirel studies the map quietly, then says: 'Your contour lines assume uniform slope between your sample points. The Thornveil has karst sinkholes — the ground drops thirty feet with no surface warning. How would you handle that?' Dax barely pauses: 'Same technique, just more sample points. It's all just measurement at the end of the day.' Lirel turns to the player with a weary expression. 'Bertrand Russell once wrote that the trouble with the world is that the stupid are cocksure and the intelligent are full of doubt. I would not call young Dax stupid, but I would note that I have mapped eleven marshlands, and the more I map, the less certain I am that I know what I am doing.'
scenario.speaker_context: Lirel is not being arrogant — she genuinely recognizes how much she still does not know about difficult terrain. Dax is not dishonest — he genuinely believes his six weeks of training have given him sufficient competence, because he does not yet know enough to see what he is missing.

structure.pattern_description: Dax's limited training gives him confidence because he cannot yet see the complexities he has not encountered. His map of Greenvale worked because Greenvale was simple terrain; he generalizes from this success to assume the Thornveil will be the same. Lirel's decades of experience have taught her how many ways mapping can go wrong, which makes her more cautious, not less. The asymmetry: low competence produces high confidence because the knowledge needed to recognize one's own gaps is the same knowledge one lacks.
structure.formal_form: Agent with low competence in domain D overestimates their competence because recognizing the limits of their knowledge requires the very knowledge they lack. Agent with high competence in D underestimates their relative standing because they assume others share their awareness of D's difficulties.
structure.why_wrong: Dax's confidence is not based on evidence that his methods will work in the Thornveil — it is based on his inability to imagine how they might fail. He does not know what karst terrain does to contour assumptions because he has never encountered it. His confidence is inversely proportional to his awareness of the problem space.
structure.counterpoint: Confidence and competence do sometimes align. A skilled person can be justifiably confident. The Dunning-Kruger pattern is specifically about the metacognitive gap: the inability to evaluate one's own performance accurately when one lacks the relevant expertise. It is not a claim that all confident people are incompetent.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dax seems eager and confident. Lirel seems cautious and uncertain. If you had to choose one of them to lead you into the Thornveil Marshes, who would you pick, and why? What does Lirel's uncertainty tell you that Dax's certainty does not?

rubric.description: Player picks Dax because he sounds more confident, or sees Lirel's caution as a sign of weakness.
Player picks Lirel based on experience but cannot articulate why Dax's confidence is misleading.
Player recognizes that Dax's confidence outstrips his experience and that Lirel's caution comes from deeper knowledge, but does not articulate the metacognitive mechanism.
Player identifies the Dunning-Kruger pattern: Dax is confident because he does not know enough to see what he is missing, while Lirel's doubt reflects awareness of genuine complexity.

Player identifies the Dunning-Kruger effect, explains the metacognitive gap (the knowledge needed to see your limits is the knowledge you lack), connects it to Russell's quote, and can describe conditions under which confidence would be a reliable signal of competence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about what Dax's training covered and what it did not. He mapped a gentle valley in good conditions. What does that experience teach him about sinkholes, shifting water tables, or terrain that changes overnight? If he has never encountered those problems, how would he know to worry about them?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the harder question: how do you tell the difference between Lirel's healthy expert humility and simple lack of confidence? If doubt can be a sign of competence, how do you avoid the opposite error — dismissing every confident person as a Dax?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dax is enthusiastic, earnest, and slightly defensive when questioned. He genuinely wants to help and does not realize his overconfidence is dangerous. Lirel is quiet, precise, and faintly amused by youthful certainty because she remembers being exactly like Dax thirty years ago.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Dax grins as you approach: 'You here to sign up for the Thornveil expedition? It'll be great — I've got my methods dialed in. Six weeks of training and I mapped a whole valley. How hard can a marsh be?'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the Dunning-Kruger pattern, Lirel nods approvingly and assigns the player to mentor Dax on the expedition's advance team. Dax initially resists but, after encountering his first sinkhole and realizing his contour method failed completely, becomes genuinely curious about what else he does not know. Lirel rewards the player with a Guild surveying kit and the observation: 'The most dangerous moment in any craft is when you first feel competent.'

scenario.context: The player is in the port town of Saltmere, where the Town Watch is debating how to allocate its limited patrol budget for the next quarter. Captain Voss has called a meeting after two dramatic wolf attacks on the coastal road last month. The Watch has data showing that pickpocketing in the market district accounts for ten times more losses than wolf attacks over the past year, but the wolf attacks were violent and widely discussed.
scenario.text: Captain Voss addresses the Watch. 'We all know what happened on the coastal road. Farmer Brek nearly lost his arm. His daughter still won't leave the house. I'm proposing we double the coastal road patrols and station archers at the Ridgeline overlook. That means pulling four officers from the market district, but the wolves are the real threat right now.' Sergeant Tully clears her throat. 'Captain, I pulled the ledger. We've had two wolf attacks this year, both last month. We've had a hundred and fourteen pickpocketing incidents in the market district in the same period. The market losses total eight times the value of livestock lost to wolves.' Voss frowns. 'Numbers on a page, Tully. I can still hear Brek screaming. The people of Saltmere need to feel safe, and right now they're terrified of wolves, not pickpockets.'
scenario.speaker_context: Captain Voss is not incompetent — he is responding to genuine fear in the community. But his resource allocation decision is being driven by the vividness and emotional salience of the wolf attacks rather than by the actual frequency and magnitude of threats.

structure.pattern_description: Voss is judging the probability and severity of threats based on how easily examples come to mind. The wolf attacks are vivid, recent, emotionally charged, and widely discussed — making them highly 'available' in memory. Pickpocketing is mundane, individually minor, and forgettable. This asymmetry in mental availability distorts his risk assessment and drives a misallocation of resources.
structure.formal_form: Agent judges frequency or probability of event type E based on the ease with which instances of E come to mind, rather than on actual base rates. Vivid, recent, or emotionally charged events are overweighted; routine, statistical, or undramatic events are underweighted.
structure.why_wrong: Two wolf attacks versus 114 pickpocketing incidents and an 8:1 loss ratio clearly indicate where the greater harm lies. Voss acknowledges the data and dismisses it because his emotional memory of the attacks feels more real than the statistics. The result is a resource allocation that protects against the rare dramatic threat while leaving the common undramatic threat unaddressed.
structure.counterpoint: Emotional salience is not always misleading. If the wolf attacks signal a new pattern (e.g., wolves driven from their territory by drought), the frequency data from the past year may understate the future risk. The error is not in taking vivid events seriously, but in letting vividness substitute for frequency analysis.

assessment.identification_prompt: Captain Voss has data from Sergeant Tully showing the market district is a much bigger problem. Why does he still want to prioritize the coastal road? What is driving his judgment if not the numbers?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Voss that wolves are the priority because the attacks were scary.
Player senses Voss might be overreacting but frames it as an emotional decision rather than a cognitive pattern.
Player identifies that Voss is weighting the dramatic events over the statistical evidence but does not name or describe the underlying mechanism.
Player identifies the availability heuristic: Voss judges threat severity by how easily and vividly the wolf attacks come to mind, overriding the base-rate data.

Player identifies the availability heuristic, explains the role of vividness, recency, and emotional charge in distorting risk assessment, and can articulate when emotional salience might legitimately signal a real change in threat level.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine you had never heard about the wolf attacks and you were just looking at the ledger numbers. Where would you put the patrols? Now ask yourself: what changed when you added the story of Farmer Brek?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now consider Voss's point about public feeling: 'The people need to feel safe.' Is there a legitimate reason to allocate some resources based on perceived rather than actual risk? Where is the line between good leadership and bad reasoning?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Captain Voss is a brave, sincere leader who takes his duty to protect Saltmere personally. He is not stupid but he trusts his gut over spreadsheets. He becomes defensive when he feels his judgment is being questioned by 'desk work.'
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: You weren't there when we pulled Brek off that road. I was. I don't need a ledger to tell me what's dangerous in my town.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the availability heuristic, Sergeant Tully backs them up with the data. Voss, after some resistance, agrees to a compromise: maintain current coastal patrols but do not strip the market district. He later admits to the player that he had been having nightmares about the wolf attacks and realizes that was coloring his judgment.

scenario.context: The player visits the Academy of Natural Philosophy in the city of Corvath, where two scholars are debating before a class of students. Professor Hale has just presented a syllogism to test the students' logical reasoning. The exercise is about evaluating the logical structure of arguments independently of whether the conclusions happen to be true.
scenario.text: Professor Hale writes on the board: 'All plants need water. Roses need water. Therefore, roses are plants.' She asks the class: 'Is this argument logically valid?' Student Tam raises his hand immediately: 'Yes, obviously. Roses are plants, and they do need water. Everything in the argument is true.' Hale then writes a second argument: 'All insects have six legs. Dogs have six legs. Therefore, dogs are insects.' She asks: 'What about this one — valid or invalid?' Tam laughs: 'Invalid, clearly. Dogs don't have six legs and they're definitely not insects.' Hale turns to the player with a slight smile. 'Interesting. My student gave opposite answers to two arguments that have exactly the same logical structure.'
scenario.speaker_context: Professor Hale is testing whether students can separate logical validity (does the conclusion follow from the premises?) from the factual truth of the conclusion. Both arguments have the same invalid form: All A are B, C is B, therefore C is A. Tam judges validity by whether the conclusion matches his beliefs.

structure.pattern_description: Tam evaluates the logical validity of arguments based on whether the conclusion aligns with what he already believes to be true, rather than by examining whether the conclusion actually follows from the premises. When the conclusion is believable (roses are plants), he accepts the argument as valid. When the conclusion is absurd (dogs are insects), he rejects it as invalid. Both arguments share the same invalid logical form.
structure.formal_form: Agent evaluates argument with structure S and conclusion C. If C matches agent's prior beliefs, agent judges the argument valid regardless of S. If C conflicts with agent's prior beliefs, agent judges the argument invalid regardless of S. The logical structure S is not evaluated independently.
structure.why_wrong: Both arguments have the form: All A are B; C is B; therefore C is A. This is the fallacy of the undistributed middle — it is invalid regardless of what A, B, and C are. The roses argument is invalid even though its conclusion happens to be true. The dogs argument is invalid and its conclusion happens to be false. Tam is not evaluating logic at all; he is checking whether conclusions match his beliefs.
structure.counterpoint: In everyday reasoning, it is often efficient to reject arguments with absurd conclusions. The error arises specifically when we are asked to evaluate logical structure and instead substitute belief-checking. Recognizing when we need to separate the two modes of evaluation is the key skill.

assessment.identification_prompt: Tam gave different answers to the two arguments. Professor Hale says they have the same logical structure. Who is right, and what is Tam actually doing when he evaluates these arguments?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Tam that the first argument is valid and the second is invalid, based on the truth of the conclusions.
Player senses something is off about Tam's reasoning but cannot identify what the two arguments have in common.
Player recognizes that both arguments might have the same structure but cannot clearly articulate why Tam's approach is wrong.
Player identifies that Tam is judging validity by whether the conclusion is believable rather than by logical structure, and recognizes both arguments share the same invalid form.

Player identifies belief bias, names the shared invalid form (undistributed middle or affirming the consequent of a categorical), explains why a true conclusion does not make an argument valid, and can construct a similar example to demonstrate the point.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Forget whether roses are actually plants. Just look at the structure: 'All A are B. C is B. Therefore C is A.' Does C being B guarantee that C is A? What if I said: 'All cats are mammals. Dogs are mammals. Therefore dogs are cats'?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now here is the practical question: in everyday life, we constantly use the plausibility of conclusions to evaluate arguments. When is that a reasonable shortcut, and when does it become the trap Tam fell into?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Professor Hale is patient, slightly mischievous, and loves setting intellectual traps that teach through surprise. She never ridicules a wrong answer but always follows up with a question that makes the student see their own error. Tam is eager and bright but overconfident in his intuitions.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Hale adjusts her spectacles and slides a piece of chalk to the player. 'My students keep telling me arguments are valid when they like the conclusion and invalid when they don't. Perhaps you can help me show them what validity actually means.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player correctly identifies belief bias, Hale invites them to construct a new pair of arguments — same form, one with a believable conclusion, one with an absurd one — to demonstrate to Tam. When Tam sees himself giving opposite answers to identical structures again, he has a genuine 'aha' moment and thanks the player. Hale offers access to the Academy's logic library.

scenario.context: The player visits the training grounds of the Silverhelm mercenary company, where Captain Renna is debriefing her squad after two recent contracts. The first contract — defending a caravan through bandit territory — was a success: no losses, bandits routed. The second contract — guarding a mine entrance — ended badly: two mercenaries injured and the mine overrun by goblins overnight. Renna is explaining both outcomes to a new recruit while the player listens.
scenario.text: Renna polishes her sword as she talks. 'The caravan job went perfectly because I read the terrain right. I positioned Kael and Dura on the ridge flanks before the bandits even showed. My instinct told me they'd hit us at the river crossing, and that's exactly where they came. Fourteen years of experience — you can't teach that.' She sets the sword down, her expression souring. 'The mine job was a disaster, but that wasn't on us. The client gave us a wrong map — the eastern tunnel wasn't even on it. And the torches they supplied were damp. You can't hold a defensive line in the dark with half your sightlines missing. If they'd given us proper intel and equipment, we'd have held that mine easily.'
scenario.speaker_context: Renna is a competent leader who genuinely believes her account of both events. She does not notice that she attributes the success entirely to her own skill and judgment while attributing the failure entirely to external factors beyond her control.

structure.pattern_description: Renna claims full personal credit for the successful caravan defense (her terrain reading, her instinct, her experience) while deflecting all responsibility for the mine failure onto external factors (bad map, damp torches, client's fault). She does not consider that the caravan success might have involved luck or favorable conditions, nor that the mine failure might have involved her own planning oversights.
structure.formal_form: When outcome is positive: agent attributes it to internal factors (skill, effort, judgment). When outcome is negative: agent attributes it to external factors (bad luck, others' mistakes, circumstances). The attribution direction is systematically self-serving.
structure.why_wrong: The asymmetry is unjustified. The caravan success may have involved favorable terrain, weak bandits, or luck in addition to Renna's skill. The mine failure may have involved Renna's failure to scout the tunnels herself or request backup torches. By consistently claiming credit for success and externalizing blame for failure, Renna cannot learn from either outcome.
structure.counterpoint: Self-serving bias is not the same as always being wrong about causes. Sometimes the leader really did make the difference, and sometimes the client really did provide bad equipment. The bias is the pattern: always internal for success, always external for failure, without examining whether each specific case warrants that attribution.

assessment.identification_prompt: Renna explains the caravan success and the mine failure. Listen to who or what she credits in each case. Do you notice a pattern in how she assigns responsibility?

rubric.description: Player accepts both explanations at face value and sees no pattern.
Player feels Renna might be making excuses about the mine but does not connect it to how she talks about the caravan.
Player notices the asymmetry — credit for success, blame elsewhere for failure — but treats it as ordinary ego rather than a systematic cognitive pattern.
Player identifies self-serving bias: Renna systematically attributes success to herself and failure to external causes, and recognizes this prevents accurate self-assessment.

Player identifies the self-serving bias, explains why the asymmetric attribution is unjustified for both outcomes, and can describe how Renna could evaluate her own performance more accurately by applying the same explanatory standards to successes and failures.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: What if you asked Renna: 'Could the caravan job have gone well partly because the bandits were poorly organized?' How do you think she'd react? Now ask: 'Could the mine job have gone badly partly because you didn't scout the tunnels yourself?' Notice anything about the difference?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the practical cost: if Renna never examines what she did right during a failure or what went lucky during a success, what happens to her planning over time? How does self-serving bias affect someone's ability to improve?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Renna is tough, experienced, and genuinely skilled — which makes her self-serving bias harder to spot because she is often right about her abilities. She is not arrogant in a cartoonish way; she simply has a blind spot about attributing outcomes. She respects directness but bristles at perceived disrespect.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Renna sizes you up as you approach. 'You want to run with the Silverhelms? Good. Let me tell you how we work. When I lead, we win. When the job goes sideways, it's because someone else cut corners. That's not ego — that's fourteen years of results.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the bias, Renna is initially defensive but a veteran squad member, Kael, backs the player up: 'Captain, you told me to skip the tunnel scout because we were short on time. Remember?' Renna goes quiet, then admits she had forgotten that decision. She offers the player a contract with the Silverhelms and begins requiring after-action reviews that examine internal factors for both wins and losses.

scenario.context: The player arrives at the Glassblower's Guild in the city of Luma, where Master Fen is attempting to teach a class of six beginners how to shape molten glass. Fen is widely regarded as the finest glassblower in the region, but his apprentices keep dropping out. The Guild Elder has asked the player to observe a lesson and figure out why.
scenario.text: Fen dips the blowpipe into the furnace and pulls out a glowing gather of molten glass. 'Right, so you just feel when the viscosity shifts — there's a moment where it goes from honey to taffy, and that's when you start your rotation. Obviously the centripetal balance has to match your breath pressure or you'll get an asymmetric bubble. Just keep it intuitive.' A student raises her hand: 'Master Fen, how do I know when the viscosity shifts? I can't tell the difference.' Fen looks genuinely puzzled. 'You just... feel it. It's obvious once you're holding it. Here — try.' The student takes the pipe, burns her hand slightly, and produces a lopsided blob. Fen stares at it, baffled. 'I don't understand. It's so straightforward. Maybe try again and just... feel it this time?' After class, the Guild Elder takes the player aside. 'He's been through nine apprentices this year. They all say the same thing: he can't explain what he does because he can't remember not knowing how to do it.'
scenario.speaker_context: Master Fen is not arrogant or impatient. He genuinely cannot understand why students struggle because the skills he has automated over decades feel obvious and natural to him. He has lost access to his own learning process.

structure.pattern_description: Fen's deep expertise has made his skills feel intuitive and self-evident. He cannot reconstruct what it was like to not understand viscosity shifts, breath pressure matching, or rotation timing, so he assumes these things are 'obvious' and 'straightforward.' His instructions reference internal sensations that only make sense to someone who already has the skill. He is not withholding information — he literally cannot see what information a beginner needs.
structure.formal_form: Agent with expertise in domain D assumes that knowledge, skills, or perceptions that feel automatic and obvious to them are equally accessible to agents without expertise in D. Agent cannot reconstruct their own pre-expertise state and therefore cannot identify what a novice needs to learn.
structure.why_wrong: Fen's teaching fails because he cannot bridge the gap between expert perception and novice perception. 'Feel when the viscosity shifts' is useless instruction to someone who has never felt it. He needs to decompose his automated skill into explicit, observable steps — but the curse of knowledge prevents him from seeing that decomposition is necessary.
structure.counterpoint: Not every communication failure is the curse of knowledge. Sometimes experts simplify correctly and the student just needs more practice. The curse specifically applies when the expert cannot identify what the student is missing because their own fluency obscures the skill's complexity.

assessment.identification_prompt: Master Fen is clearly a brilliant glassblower. His students keep quitting. The Guild Elder says the problem is that Fen 'can't remember not knowing.' What does that mean, exactly, and how does it show up in his teaching?

rubric.description: Player blames the students for lack of talent or effort, or blames Fen for being arrogant.
Player recognizes Fen is a bad teacher but attributes it to impatience or poor communication skills in general.
Player identifies that Fen's instructions are too vague for beginners but does not connect this to his expertise making skills feel obvious.

Player identifies the curse of knowledge: Fen's expertise makes his skills feel self-evident, so he cannot identify what a novice needs to be told, and his instructions assume knowledge the students do not have.

Player identifies the curse of knowledge, explains the mechanism (expertise automates skills until they feel obvious, erasing memory of the learning process), and can suggest concrete strategies for overcoming it (having Fen teach alongside a recent apprentice who still remembers the struggles, decomposing steps explicitly, watching where students fail and reverse-engineering what was left unsaid).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Think about something you're really good at — something that feels natural and easy. Now imagine trying to explain it to someone who has never done it. Would you be able to list every tiny step, or would you say something like 'you just feel it'? What's happening when you say that?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here's the what-if: suppose you gave Fen a detailed, step-by-step script written by a former apprentice who struggled and eventually learned. Would Fen follow it? Or would he keep going off-script because the steps seem 'unnecessarily complicated' to him? What does that tell you about how hard the curse is to break even when you know about it?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Fen is gentle, earnest, and increasingly distressed that his students keep failing. He takes their failures personally but cannot figure out what he is doing wrong. He is a perfectionist who speaks about glass with unconscious poetry and assumes everyone sees what he sees in the molten material.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Fen looks up from the furnace with tired eyes. 'Another one quit yesterday. She said I don't explain things. But I do explain — I tell them exactly what to do. Feel the glass, read the color, match your breath. What else is there to say?'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the curse of knowledge, they can propose a solution: pair Fen with his one surviving apprentice, Mira, who is six months in and still remembers her early confusion. Mira translates Fen's expert intuitions into step-by-step instructions. Fen watches a new student succeed using Mira's translations and finally understands what he has been missing. He rewards the player with a hand-blown glass lens that reveals hidden inscriptions throughout the game world.

scenario.context: The player encounters a group of settlers at the frontier outpost of Briarwatch. The settlers are preparing to cross the Ashfall Waste — a three-day desert crossing — to reach fertile land on the other side. The outpost quartermaster, Hesta, is reviewing their supply plan. Every previous expedition she has provisioned has taken five to seven days due to sandstorms, broken axles, and navigation errors in the featureless terrain.
scenario.text: Hesta examines the settlers' supply list and frowns. 'You've packed three days of water per person. The crossing is rated at three days, yes — but in the twelve expeditions I've provisioned, not one has made it in three. The fastest was five days. The slowest was nine.' The expedition leader, Jorin, smiles confidently. 'Those groups didn't have our navigator. And we repacked the wagons to reduce weight. We'll move faster than anyone before us. Three days of water is plenty — maybe we'll even have some left over.' Hesta looks at the player. 'Every leader who has sat in that chair has told me some version of what Jorin just said. They all had a reason why they would be the exception. None of them were.'
scenario.speaker_context: Jorin is not naive — he has made genuine preparations. But he is estimating his own expedition's outcome based on the best-case scenario rather than the base rate of past expeditions, and he believes his specific circumstances exempt him from the historical pattern.

structure.pattern_description: Jorin overestimates the likelihood of a favorable outcome (three-day crossing) and underestimates the likelihood of setbacks, despite strong base-rate evidence (zero out of twelve expeditions have achieved three days). He does this by focusing on case-specific factors (good navigator, lighter wagons) that he believes make him exceptional, while ignoring that every previous leader also had case-specific reasons for optimism.
structure.formal_form: Agent estimates probability of positive outcome P+ for their own situation as higher than the base rate warrants, typically by identifying case-specific factors that they believe make them exceptional. Base-rate evidence of P- is acknowledged but discounted as applying to 'other people' or 'other circumstances.'
structure.why_wrong: Twelve out of twelve previous expeditions took longer than three days. Jorin's belief that his navigator and lighter wagons will overcome the pattern is exactly the kind of reasoning every previous leader used. The base rate is not a suggestion — it reflects the actual distribution of outcomes for this crossing, including expeditions that also had good navigators and light wagons.
structure.counterpoint: Optimism is not always irrational. If Jorin had genuinely novel technology (say, a reliable compass in a region where magnetic anomalies cause navigation errors), he might have legitimate reason to expect a better outcome. The bias is in discounting the base rate without proportionate evidence for why this case is truly different.

assessment.identification_prompt: Jorin has good reasons for confidence — a skilled navigator and lighter wagons. But Hesta says every previous leader also had reasons for confidence. Who should you believe, and why?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Jorin that his preparations are sufficient and three days is realistic.
Player thinks Jorin might be underestimating the risk but cannot articulate why his confidence is misplaced given his preparations.
Player recognizes the base rate (0 out of 12 made it in three days) is concerning but does not explain why Jorin's case-specific reasoning is insufficient to override it.
Player identifies optimism bias: Jorin believes he is the exception to a strong base rate, using the same type of case-specific reasoning that every previous leader used.

Player identifies optimism bias, explains the mechanism (case-specific reasoning overriding base rates), notes that previous leaders also had reasons for optimism, and can articulate what kind of evidence would actually justify deviating from the base rate.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Imagine you're the thirteenth expedition leader. You also have good reasons to be confident. But so did the twelfth, and the eleventh, and the tenth. At what point does 'I'm different' stop being a reason and start being a pattern?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Now consider: Jorin's optimism might actually help the expedition. Confident leaders make decisive calls under pressure. Is there a way to be realistically prepared (pack seven days of water) while still being psychologically optimistic? Or does correcting the bias necessarily undermine morale?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jorin is charismatic, decisive, and genuinely skilled — the kind of leader people want to follow. His optimism is partly what makes him effective, which makes the bias harder to challenge because it is intertwined with his genuine strengths. Hesta is dry, data-driven, and deeply tired of watching confident people underpack.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Jorin claps you on the shoulder. 'Hesta means well, but she's a worrier. She's never actually made the crossing herself — she just sits here counting water jugs. We've done our homework. Three days. You'll see.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the optimism bias, Jorin resists but Hesta backs the player with the ledger showing all twelve previous expeditions. The player can broker a compromise: Jorin keeps his confident leadership style but packs five days of water. The crossing takes five and a half days due to a sandstorm. Jorin, humbled, thanks the player at the far side and admits: 'I really did think we'd be the exception.'

scenario.context: The player visits the farming village of Greymoor, which has been hit by two consecutive bad harvests. The village council is debating whether to invest their remaining savings in a new irrigation system. Engineer Dalla has presented a detailed plan showing that the irrigation system would stabilize yields even in dry years, and the regional agricultural records show that three consecutive bad harvests have never occurred in two hundred years of record-keeping. But Elder Sorn, who lived through a famine as a child, dominates the discussion.
scenario.text: Elder Sorn grips the edge of the council table. 'Two bad harvests in a row. It will be three — I can feel it. And if we spend our savings on Dalla's pipes and ditches, we'll have nothing left when the third failure comes. No food, no coin, nothing. We should bury the gold, ration what grain we have, and pray.' Dalla responds calmly: 'Elder Sorn, the records show—' Sorn cuts her off. 'Records! The records didn't predict the last two failures either. Things are getting worse. The soil is dying. Even if we build the irrigation, something else will go wrong — it always does. A flood, a blight, locusts. We should prepare for the worst and hope I'm wrong.' Dalla looks to the player. 'The irrigation plan costs sixty percent of our reserves and produces returns within one season. Even in the worst drought on record, irrigated fields in the next valley yielded seventy percent of normal. But Elder Sorn sees only catastrophe.'
scenario.speaker_context: Elder Sorn is not stupid — he survived a real famine and his fear is rooted in genuine trauma. But his expectation of negative outcomes has detached from the evidence. He is overweighting the probability of continued disaster and underweighting the evidence for the irrigation system's effectiveness.

structure.pattern_description: Sorn systematically overestimates the likelihood of negative outcomes (three consecutive bad harvests, irrigation failure, additional disasters) while dismissing evidence of positive possibilities (historical base rates, irrigation data from the next valley, Dalla's engineering analysis). His trauma-driven expectation of catastrophe leads him to reject an investment that the evidence supports, preferring inaction and hoarding as the 'safe' choice — even though inaction carries its own risks.
structure.formal_form: Agent overestimates probability of negative outcomes P- and underestimates probability of positive outcomes P+, leading to risk-averse decisions that are not justified by the available evidence. Negative possibilities are treated as near-certainties; positive evidence is dismissed as unreliable or insufficient.
structure.why_wrong: The historical record shows no precedent for three consecutive failures. The irrigation data from a neighboring valley demonstrates effectiveness even in severe drought. Sorn dismisses both sources of evidence with vague catastrophizing ('something else will go wrong, it always does'). His plan — bury the gold and ration — actually increases the risk of famine by forgoing the investment that would stabilize food supply.
structure.counterpoint: Pessimism can be adaptive when the downside risk is catastrophic and irreversible. If spending the reserves on irrigation and having it fail would mean starvation with no recovery option, Sorn's caution has a rational kernel. The bias is in treating every possible negative outcome as likely while treating every positive outcome as unlikely, regardless of the evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: Elder Sorn has real experience with famine, and his fear is understandable. But Dalla has data and a plan. What is driving Sorn's opposition — is it the evidence, or something else?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Sorn that things will get worse and the village should save its money.
Player thinks Sorn is being too cautious but attributes it to his personality rather than a cognitive pattern.
Player recognizes Sorn is overestimating the risk but does not connect it to the systematic underweighting of positive evidence.
Player identifies pessimism bias: Sorn overestimates negative outcomes and dismisses positive evidence, and his trauma is driving the distortion rather than the data.

Player identifies pessimism bias, explains how Sorn's trauma amplifies negative expectations beyond what evidence supports, recognizes that his 'safe' plan of inaction carries its own risks, and can articulate when caution is genuinely warranted versus when it is the bias talking.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Sorn says 'something else will go wrong — it always does.' Does it always? What does the two-hundred-year record actually show? And consider: if the village does nothing and a third bad harvest comes anyway, are they better or worse off than if they had built the irrigation?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Good. Now here is the tension: Sorn's pessimism comes from surviving a real famine. His fear is not irrational — it is disproportionate. How do you respect someone's lived experience while still pointing out that their fear is distorting their judgment? Is there a way to honour what Sorn knows without letting it dictate policy?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Elder Sorn is not a villain — he is a traumatized survivor whose protective instincts have calcified into reflexive catastrophizing. He speaks with quiet intensity and invokes his famine memories as moral authority. He is respected in the village, which makes his pessimism influential. Dalla is pragmatic, data-oriented, and frustrated but not dismissive of Sorn's experience.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Sorn fixes you with hollow eyes. 'You're young. You've never watched a village eat its seed grain because there was nothing else. I have. When I tell you it's going to get worse, I'm not guessing. I'm remembering.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the pessimism bias, they can broker a compromise: invest in the irrigation system but keep a forty-percent reserve as Sorn's emergency fund. When the irrigation works and the next harvest comes in strong, Sorn admits he was wrong about the outcome — but adds, quietly, 'I'll never stop worrying. That's what surviving does to you.' The player gains the village's trust and access to Dalla's engineering workshop.

scenario.context: The player visits the Merchant Council of Thornport, where Guildmaster Venn is deciding whether to renew the trade contract with a caravan company called the Dustwalkers. The Dustwalkers have completed forty-seven out of fifty contracts successfully over three years — a 94% success rate. But Venn is fixated on the three failures.
scenario.text: Guildmaster Venn tosses the contract renewal onto the table. 'I'm not signing this. The Dustwalkers lost an entire shipment of silkwood last autumn. Before that, they were late by two weeks on the dye delivery — two weeks! Cost us the Midsummer Fair orders. And the year before, they let a crate of glassware get smashed on the mountain pass. Three disasters in three years.' His trade secretary, Maren, clears her throat. 'Guildmaster, those are three incidents out of fifty contracts. The other forty-seven arrived on time and intact. Their reliability rate is ninety-four percent — higher than any other company we've used. The next best is the Ironwheel Guild at eighty-one percent.' Venn shakes his head. 'I don't care about the forty-seven. I remember the silkwood. I remember explaining to Lord Ashcroft why his glass was in pieces. The bad ones stick with you, Maren.'
scenario.speaker_context: Venn is not being irrational in isolation — each failure did cause real harm. But he is giving the three negative events disproportionate weight relative to the forty-seven positive ones, and he is about to make a decision that would replace a 94% reliable partner with an 81% reliable one.

structure.pattern_description: Venn's memory and emotional weighting are dominated by the three failures. He can recall each one vividly — the silkwood, the dye delay, the smashed glassware — but the forty-seven successes have faded into an undifferentiated background. The negative events carry disproportionate influence on his judgment, leading him to characterize a 94% success rate as unacceptable and consider switching to a measurably worse alternative.
structure.formal_form: Agent gives disproportionate weight to negative events E- relative to positive events E+ of comparable or greater magnitude. Negative events are more memorable, more emotionally vivid, and more influential on decisions than an equivalent number or magnitude of positive events.
structure.why_wrong: Three failures out of fifty contracts is a 6% failure rate. Replacing the Dustwalkers with the next-best option (81% reliability) would mean roughly ten failures per fifty contracts instead of three. Venn's emotional response to the negative events is leading him toward a decision that will produce more of exactly the outcomes he wants to avoid.
structure.counterpoint: Negativity bias has evolutionary roots — threats deserve more attention than routine safety. In some contexts, a single failure can be catastrophic enough to outweigh many successes (e.g., a bridge engineer). The bias becomes a problem when the negative events are not catastrophic but are treated as if they are, or when the comparison to alternatives is ignored.

assessment.identification_prompt: Venn says 'the bad ones stick with you.' He's right that the failures were real problems. But is he making a good decision by dropping the Dustwalkers? What is he not accounting for?

rubric.description: Player agrees with Venn that three failures are unacceptable and the Dustwalkers should be dropped.
Player senses Venn might be overreacting but cannot articulate why the failures feel so much bigger than the successes.
Player recognizes the 94% success rate is strong but does not explain why Venn is weighting the negatives so heavily or what the consequence of switching would be.
Player identifies negativity bias: the three failures loom larger in Venn's memory and emotional response than the forty-seven successes, and switching to a worse provider would increase failures.

Player identifies negativity bias, explains the asymmetry in how negative and positive events are weighted in memory and decision-making, calculates or estimates the comparative failure rates, and can articulate when heightened sensitivity to negatives is appropriate versus when it distorts judgment.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Venn wants to switch to the Ironwheel Guild at eighty-one percent reliability. Out of fifty contracts, how many failures would that be? Is that more or fewer than three? What does that tell you about whether switching actually solves Venn's problem?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Now consider: Venn says 'the bad ones stick with you.' He's describing how his own memory works. If you know your brain overweights negatives, what systems or practices could you put in place to counteract that when making business decisions?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Venn is a shrewd, experienced merchant who prides himself on high standards. He is not emotional in general, which makes his negativity bias harder to spot — it presents as rigorous quality control rather than irrational fear. Maren is his long-suffering trade secretary who keeps the actual numbers and quietly despairs when he ignores them.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Venn slides the contract across the table toward you. 'You're a traveller — you've used caravan companies. Would you trust a company that lost your cargo three times? I don't care what the numbers say. I remember what went wrong.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies the negativity bias, Maren produces a comparative ledger showing the Dustwalkers against every other company. The numbers are unambiguous. Venn, confronted with the data in context, grudgingly renews the contract but adds penalty clauses for future failures. He tells the player: 'You're right, and I hate it. The ones that go wrong just feel bigger.' He offers the player a merchant's discount at Thornport shops.

scenario.context: The player gains access to the War Council of the city-state of Valdris, which is planning a pre-emptive strike on the neighbouring city of Korrath. The Council has been meeting in closed sessions for three weeks. Initially, several members had reservations, but by now the group has reached enthusiastic unanimous agreement. The player arrives as an outside advisor just before the final vote.
scenario.text: General Tova stands before a map bristling with pins. 'The plan is set. We strike at dawn in twelve days. Cavalry through the Ashford Gap, infantry along the river road, sappers through the old mine tunnels. Every member of this council has reviewed the plan and every member agrees: this is our moment.' She looks around the table. 'Does anyone wish to raise a final concern?' Silence. The player notices Lord Caelen shift uncomfortably in his seat but say nothing. After the session, the player catches Caelen in the corridor. He glances around nervously. 'You want the truth? The mine tunnels haven't been surveyed in eight years. We don't know if they're passable. I raised this in the second meeting and Tova said I was undermining morale. Councillor Drace told me that if I couldn't commit to the group, I should resign. After that... I stopped talking. We all stopped talking. Miren had concerns about the cavalry timing. She stopped too. Now everyone nods and smiles and says the plan is brilliant. It might be. But nobody has stress-tested it because nobody is allowed to ask hard questions anymore.'
scenario.speaker_context: The War Council has not reached genuine consensus through rigorous debate. Dissent was socially punished in early meetings, and members self-censored to maintain group harmony. The unanimity is an artifact of conformity pressure, not of the plan's actual soundness.

structure.pattern_description: The War Council exhibits classic groupthink: (1) the illusion of unanimity — silence is read as agreement; (2) direct pressure on dissenters — Caelen was accused of undermining morale and threatened with expulsion; (3) self-censorship — Caelen and Miren stopped raising concerns; (4) the illusion of invulnerability — 'this is our moment' suggests overconfidence. The result is a plan that has not been stress-tested because the social dynamics of the group prevent critical evaluation.
structure.formal_form: A cohesive group under directive leadership suppresses dissent through social pressure, self-censorship, and conformity norms, producing an illusion of unanimous agreement. The group's decision-making quality degrades because alternative viewpoints, risks, and counterarguments are never voiced or examined.
structure.why_wrong: The plan may have serious flaws (unsurveyed tunnels, questionable cavalry timing) that will only become apparent during execution, when the cost of failure is catastrophic. The council's unanimity does not reflect the actual distribution of opinions or concerns — it reflects the social cost of dissenting. A plan that cannot survive internal criticism is unlikely to survive contact with the enemy.
structure.counterpoint: Group cohesion is not inherently bad — military planning requires trust and commitment. The problem is when cohesion suppresses critical evaluation. Effective military councils historically used designated devil's advocates or red teams precisely to get the benefits of cohesion without the costs of groupthink.

assessment.identification_prompt: The War Council has reached unanimous agreement on the plan. General Tova seems confident that everyone is on board. But Lord Caelen tells you a different story. What is actually happening in this council, and why does unanimous agreement not mean the plan is sound?

rubric.description: Player takes the unanimity at face value and sees nothing wrong with the council's process.
Player recognizes that Caelen has been silenced but treats it as ordinary bullying or personality conflict rather than a systemic group dynamic.
Player identifies that dissent has been suppressed and the unanimity is false, but does not articulate the broader pattern or its consequences for decision quality.
Player identifies groupthink: social pressure and self-censorship have created an illusion of consensus, and the plan has not been critically evaluated because dissent is punished.

Player identifies groupthink, names multiple symptoms (illusion of unanimity, pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, illusion of invulnerability), explains how these degrade decision quality, and can propose structural remedies (devil's advocate, anonymous concern-raising, red-teaming the plan).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: General Tova asked if anyone had concerns and nobody spoke. But Caelen told you he does have concerns — and so does Miren. If they have concerns but won't voice them, what does the silence actually tell you? Is it agreement or something else?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Here is the what-if: suppose you advise General Tova to appoint a devil's advocate — someone whose official job is to argue against the plan. Tova might say: 'That will weaken our resolve and waste time.' How would you respond? What is the cost of artificial dissent versus the cost of real but invisible doubt?

game_hooks.npc_personality: General Tova is a charismatic, decisive commander who values loyalty and unity. She is not a tyrant — she genuinely believes consensus means the plan is strong. She does not realize that she has created an environment where disagreement feels disloyal. Lord Caelen is thoughtful and courageous on the battlefield but conflict-averse in social settings. He knows the council is broken but fears the personal cost of saying so.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Caelen pulls you into an alcove and speaks barely above a whisper. 'Everyone in that room has doubts. I know because we used to talk freely at the first meetings. Then Tova shut me down and Drace threatened to have me removed. Now we all just nod. The plan might work — but nobody has tried to break it, and that terrifies me more than Korrath does.'
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player identifies groupthink and proposes a structural solution (devil's advocate, anonymous written concerns, red team exercise), Caelen agrees to back the player in the next session. The player can present the concept to Tova, who initially resists but relents when Caelen and Miren finally voice their concerns. The red team exercise reveals the unsurveyed tunnels are partially collapsed, saving the plan from a fatal flaw. Tova, shaken, thanks the player and institutes a permanent red team for future war councils. The player gains Caelen and Miren as allies for future missions.
